body.text: The United Nations’ top court has found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against the Rohingya ethnic group during military assaults in 2017.

“This is a historic ruling,” Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group, said in an email. “For the first time, the world court has found a state responsible for committing genocide – and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president.”

Min Aung Hlaing, the military chief who led a coup in 2021 that plunged Myanmar into a civil conflict that still rages, was in 2017 the commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military, the Tatmadaw. In April of this year, he transitioned from military leadership to the political arena, rising to the presidency following general elections widely described as a “sham.”

In announcing the court’s 9-6 decision, International Court of Justice (ICJ) President Judge Yuji Iwasawa said it had found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

Iwasawa said that during a fierce “clearance operation” in Rakhine State in 2017, Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of members of the Rohingya minority Muslim population and committed widespread sexual violence.

“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”

Iwasawa also spoke of the ways in which restriction against the Rohingya group, such as special marriage permission requirements and limits on the number of children married couples were allowed to have, impacted birth rates.

The U.N. Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, more simply known as the Genocide Convention, was unanimously adopted in 1948 by an international community horrified by the Holocaust. The convention defines genocide as any of five “acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.” Those acts include killing, causing serious harm, inflicting destructive living conditions, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children.
The convention went into effect in 1951, becoming the first U.N. human rights treaty.

The Gambia, a predominantly Muslim country, filed a case at the ICJ with the support of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in 2019, accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya. At a hearing in January, The Gambia’s Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya of western Myanmar were “targeted for destruction” by the country’s government during a brutal military operation in 2017.

The operation drove an estimated 750,000 desperate people over the border into Bangladesh, where most still remain in large refugee camps. United Nations investigators later said that the offensives showed “genocidal intent,” while Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein, the then U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, described the situation as a “textbook example of ethnic cleansing.” Since the beginning of the ICJ case in 2019, Myanmar has defended its actions on the grounds that it was defending itself against attacks by Rohingya militant groups.

The ICJ dismissed that claim. While the court acknowledged that military operations happened in areas where militant attacks had occurred, the ICJ said that the military’s response was so excessive – including the targeted killing of children and babies, and methodical burning of entire villages – that it could not credibly be characterized as a counterinsurgency operation. “[T]he execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, including gang and mass rape, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counter-insurgency operations,” the court ruled.

Today’s verdict brings to an end to a case that could have significant implications for future genocide cases. While dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for committing genocide, no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of doing so.

In a piece for The Diplomat, Lucky Karim, a Rohingya human rights activist and founder of Refugee Women for Peace and Justice (RWPJ), wrote, “This historic ruling offers a moment of vindication and solace for the nearly 2 million of us who fled our homes in 2017, and for those who continue to languish in tiny shelters in refugee camps, hoping for their rights to be restored, justice to be served, and to return home.”

Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court, told the BBC prior to the hearing that a guilty verdict would be “a judgement of landmark importance.” He said, “It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state.”

As many observers have noted, this is likely to have implications for other genocide cases before the ICJ, in particular one brought by South Africa against Israel over the war in Gaza in 2024. Israel has described the case as “wholly unfounded” and based on “biased and false claims.”

Despite the historic ruling, the ICJ has no means of enforcing its verdict. Crisis Group’s Horsey noted, “What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyidaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it.”

China in particular has consistently vetoed United Nations Security Council resolutions to condemn Myanmar for its human rights violations, both before and after the 2021 military coup. Of note in that regard, the sole ICJ judge from China, Xue Hanqin, found Myanmar not guilty of every charge. In two specific findings (that Myanmar “has violated its obligation to punish genocide” and failed to “enact the necessary legislation to give effect” to the Genocide Convention) Xue was the only judge to dissent in 14-1 rulings.
Karim urged the U.N. member states to ensure that the ICJ’s judgement is “more than a piece of paper.”
“They must use this judgement to hold the Myanmar military accountable for its crimes and pursue every possible means to protect and aid Rohingya,” she wrote.
